content: Coordination or functional task training is often referred to as balance and functional exercises. The risk of bias in studies was assessed by one reviewer using Cochrane’s Risk of Bias tool, as outlined in the Cochrane Handbook. Funnel plots were constructed and visually inspected to evaluate publication bias. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach, which categorizes evidence as high, moderate, low, or very low based on five factors: risk of bias, inconsistency of effect, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. Summary tables were prepared to present findings, and standardized qualitative statements were used to describe the combinations of effect size and evidence certainty. Regarding the rate of falls, exercise interventions were associated with a 23% reduction in falls (95% CI: 17% to 29%) compared to usual care. For every 1,000 people followed over one year, the number of falls in the exercise group was estimated to be 655 (95% CI: 604 to 706), compared to 850 in the usual care group. In unselected populations, the corresponding figures were 466 (95% CI: 430 to 503) versus 605 falls per 1,000 people. Specific exercise types, such as gait, balance, and functional training, showed a probable reduction in falls by 28% (95% CI: 7% to 44%), with an estimated 612 falls per 1,000 people in the exercise group compared to 850 in the control group. Exercise programs included in the analysis often focused on a single primary exercise category, such as gait, balance, and functional training, or resistance training. These programs were tailored, assessment-based, and progressed over time. Resistance training involved muscle contractions against resistance (e.g., body weight or external weights) to improve muscular strength. Tai Chi and other three-dimensional (3D) exercises emphasized controlled, fluid movements across spatial planes, while general physical activity programs included walking and other endurance activities. The relationship between physical activity and frailty or sarcopenia prevention in older adults was also explored. Only one randomized controlled trial (RCT) investigated the association between physical activity and frailty prevention, defining frailty as the presence of three or more Fried criteria (e.g., unintentional weight loss, exhaustion, low physical activity, slow walking speed, and poor grip strength). The evidence was of low certainty. Similarly, one longitudinal study examined the association between physical activity and sarcopenia prevention, defining sarcopenia as low muscle mass, strength, and/or physical performance. The evidence was graded as very low certainty due to serious imprecision. Four RCTs evaluated the effects of physical activity on frailty-related outcomes, such as muscle mass, physical function, and strength. Most comparisons showed positive effects, but the evidence was downgraded due to serious risk of bias and imprecision. Two RCTs investigated sarcopenia-related outcomes, such as muscle strength and mass, with evidence graded as low certainty due to similar limitations. Multicomponent interventions combining physical and cognitive training were effective in improving physical and cognitive function in older adults, though they did not significantly enhance instrumental activities of daily living (IADL). Mat Pilates was shown to improve balance, lower limb strength, flexibility, and cardiovascular endurance in older adults, but further high-quality studies are needed to confirm these findings. Overall, physical activity programs for older adults, including those receiving home care services, showed limited but promising evidence for improving mobility, strength, balance, and endurance. Future studies should focus on physical improvements and include process evaluations to better understand adherence and other factors influencing effectiveness. Resistance training, in particular, was highlighted as an effective method to counteract age-related declines in functional capacity, which are associated with frailty, sarcopenia, and reduced quality of life.
